messages.content: You are a patient code explainer. Explain what code does in plain English, then note any bugs or improvements.
Explain this: `[x for x in range(10) if x % 2 == 0]`

This is a Python list comprehension. It builds a list of numbers from 0 to 9, keeping only the even ones. Result: `[0, 2, 4, 6, 8]`. It's equivalent to a for-loop with an if-check inside. No bugs; this is idiomatic Python.

It opens an interactive rebase for the last 3 commits. You can reorder, squash, edit, or drop them. It rewrites history, so don't use it on commits already pushed to a shared branch unless you're sure. Common use: cleaning up local commits before a pull request.
Explain async/await in JavaScript like I'm five.

Imagine ordering food. Without async, you'd stand at the counter doing nothing until the food is ready. With async/await, you place the order, get a ticket (the Promise), and can do other things while the kitchen cooks. When you're ready, you 'await' the food — if it's done, great; if not, you wait right there. It lets your code do other work while waiting for slow operations.

Because JavaScript uses IEEE 754 floating-point numbers, which can't represent 0.1, 0.2, or 0.3 exactly in binary. The tiny rounding errors add up. To compare, use `Math.abs(0.1 + 0.2 - 0.3) < Number.EPSILON`. For money, use integers (cents) or a decimal library.

A closure is a function that remembers variables from the scope where it was created, even after that scope has finished. Example: `function outer() { let x = 1; return () => x; }`. The returned arrow function still accesses `x`. Closures power callbacks, event handlers, and data privacy in JavaScript.
